q: Specific defence, which develops during life after contact with particular antigens, is also called:
x: Specific defence is acquired or adaptive: it develops after exposure to a particular antigen or vaccine. Innate, non-specific defences are present from birth and act the same way against all invaders.

q: A lymphocyte is described as immunocompetent when it:
o: Has lost its nucleus and carries oxygen
Can engulf any pathogen it meets
Is able to divide only once
Has receptors that let it recognise and respond to one particular antigen
x: Immunocompetence means the lymphocyte has matured and carries surface receptors for a specific antigen, so it can respond to it. Engulfing any pathogen is the non-specific job of phagocytes.

q: Lymphocytes, the main cells of the specific immune response, are a kind of:
x: Lymphocytes are white blood cells (agranulocytes) found in blood, lymph and lymphoid organs.

q: Each B lymphocyte carries surface receptors that can bind:
o: Any antigen that enters the body
x: Every B cell has many copies of one receptor, which fits one antigen only. That is why only a few B cells respond to any given antigen.

q: Plasma cells are packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum because they:
o: Make and secrete large amounts of antibody protein
x: Antibodies are proteins made on ribosomes of the rough ER, and a plasma cell secretes thousands of them per second, so it needs a very large amount of rough ER.

q: Antibodies are also known as:
x: Antibodies are immunoglobulins (Ig), proteins such as IgG and IgM. Antigens are the foreign molecules that antibodies bind.

q: Antibody-mediated immunity is called humoral immunity because the antibodies:
o: Circulate in body fluids such as plasma and lymph
Stay attached to the cells that made them
Are made only in the brain
x: 'Humour' is an old word for body fluid. Antibodies are released into plasma, lymph and other fluids, where they act on antigens.

q: After a B cell is activated, some of its daughter cells do not secrete antibody at once but live for years. These are:
x: Memory B cells stay in the body long after the infection and respond quickly if the same antigen returns. Plasma cells secrete antibody straight away but are short-lived.

q: Memory cells, which allow a faster response on a second infection, are formed by:
x: Activated B cells give rise to memory B cells and activated T cells give rise to memory T cells, so both arms of the specific response have memory.

q: Besides virus-infected cells, cytotoxic T cells can also destroy:
o: The body's normal red blood cells
x: Cytotoxic T cells recognise and kill body cells showing abnormal or foreign antigens, such as cancer cells. Healthy self cells are normally left alone.

q: The chemical messengers released by helper T cells to activate other lymphocytes are called:
x: Helper T cells release cytokines, such as interleukins, that stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Antibodies come from plasma cells and histamine from mast cells.

q: Each of the two arms of a Y-shaped antibody molecule is formed by:
o: One heavy chain and two light chains
One light chain and part of one heavy chain
x: An antibody has two heavy and two light chains. Each arm consists of a whole light chain alongside the upper part of a heavy chain; the stem is formed by the two heavy chains alone.

q: An antibody binds to its antigen because:
o: Both are made of the same nucleic acid
Their shapes are complementary, fitting like a lock and key
The antibody digests the antigen with enzymes
Any antibody can attach to any antigen
x: The antigen-binding site has a shape complementary to one antigenic determinant, so binding is specific, like a key in a lock. Antibodies do not digest antigens.

q: Coating of a bacterium with antibodies, so that phagocytes engulf it more readily, is called:
x: In opsonisation antibodies act as markers on the pathogen's surface that phagocytes recognise. Agglutination is clumping, neutralisation is blocking a toxin, and precipitation is forming insoluble complexes.

q: Most antigens are:
o: Small ions such as sodium and chloride
Large molecules such as proteins and polysaccharides
x: Antigens are usually large molecules, chiefly proteins and polysaccharides on the surfaces of pathogens or foreign cells. Small ions and simple sugars do not trigger an immune response.

q: While T cells mature in the thymus, those that react strongly against the body's own antigens are:
o: Released into the blood as cytotoxic T cells
Destroyed, so the mature T cells tolerate self
x: Self-reactive T cells are removed during maturation. This self-tolerance stops the immune system from attacking the body's own tissues.

q: The injected (Salk) polio vaccine contains:
x: The Salk vaccine uses inactivated virus and is given by injection. The oral Sabin vaccine uses live weakened virus.

q: In active immunity, the antibodies that protect the person are:
o: Received from another person or an animal
Received only from the mother's milk
Made by that person's own lymphocytes
x: Active immunity means the person's own B cells respond and make antibodies, which also produces memory cells. Antibodies received from another source give passive immunity.

q: An allergy is best described as:
o: A failure to make any antibodies
An excessive immune response to a normally harmless substance
An immune attack on the body's own cells
Immunity passed from mother to baby
x: In an allergy the immune system overreacts to harmless substances such as pollen or dust. Attacking one's own cells is autoimmunity.

q: Anaphylactic shock is:
o: A mild skin rash that fades in minutes
A sudden, severe allergic reaction affecting the whole body that can be life-threatening
x: Anaphylaxis is a rapid, whole-body allergic reaction, for example to a bee sting or a drug. Blood pressure can fall and breathing become difficult, so it is a medical emergency.

q: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys the:
o: Red blood cells in the spleen
Helper T cells in the blood
Insulin-secreting beta cells of the pancreas
x: In type 1 diabetes, the body's own lymphocytes attack the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans, so little insulin is made. Glucagon comes from alpha cells of the pancreas, not the liver.

q: For an organ transplant, a close relative is often preferred as donor because relatives are more likely to have:
o: Similar tissue antigens on their cells
No antigens on their cells at all
x: Rejection happens when the recipient's T cells recognise foreign tissue antigens. Relatives share more genes, so their tissue antigens are more alike and rejection is less likely.

q: If blood group A is transfused into a person of blood group B, the donor red cells clump because the recipient's plasma contains:
x: A group B person carries anti-A antibodies in plasma. These bind the A antigens on the donated cells and agglutinate them.

q: Antigen recognition depends on receptor molecules on the cell surface. Such receptors are present on:
x: Both kinds of lymphocyte have surface receptors for a specific antigen: B-cell receptors are membrane antibodies, and T cells have T-cell receptors.

q: Plasma cells develop from:
x: When a B cell meets its antigen it divides, and many of its offspring become antibody-secreting plasma cells. T cells do not form plasma cells.

q: Which of these white blood cells attacks every invader in the same way, and so does NOT take part in specific defence?
x: Neutrophils are phagocytes that attack any invader in the same way, so they are part of non-specific defence. Plasma cells, helper T cells and memory B cells all act against particular antigens.

q: A single plasma cell secretes antibodies that are:
o: Of every kind, against all antigens
All of one kind, specific for one antigen
Of a new kind every hour
x: A plasma cell comes from one B-cell clone, so all the antibody it secretes has the same binding site and fits the same antigen.

q: Vaccines are given before a person meets the disease mainly because:
o: Active immunity takes days to weeks to develop
Vaccines cure a disease that has already started
Vaccines work only in sick people
x: A vaccine makes the body produce its own antibodies and memory cells, and this takes time. Given in advance, it ensures protection is ready when the real pathogen arrives.

q: An attenuated vaccine contains pathogens that are:
o: Alive but weakened so that they do not cause the disease
Dead and broken into small pieces
x: Attenuated means weakened. The live organisms can still stimulate the immune system but cannot cause the illness in healthy people.

q: Louis Pasteur is known for developing a vaccine against:
x: Pasteur developed vaccines against rabies and anthrax. Jenner's work was on smallpox, Salk and Sabin made polio vaccines, and BCG is for tuberculosis.

q: Humoral immunity is mainly effective against:
o: Viruses that are hidden inside body cells
Bacteria and toxins circulating in the body fluids
x: Antibodies act in plasma and lymph, so they deal best with free bacteria, viruses outside cells and toxins. Infected cells, cancer cells and grafts are mainly handled by T cells.

q: A vaccine contains antigens, whereas an antiserum used for treatment contains:
x: A vaccine stimulates the body to make its own antibodies (active immunity). An antiserum supplies ready-made antibodies (passive immunity).

q: The immune system tells 'self' from 'non-self' mainly by recognising:
o: Molecules (antigens) on the surfaces of cells
The number of nuclei in the cells
x: Body cells carry their own surface molecules that the immune system tolerates. Foreign cells and pathogens carry different surface antigens that lymphocytes recognise.

q: Unlike B cells, T cells recognise an antigen only when it is:
o: Bound to a red blood cell
Displayed on the surface of a body cell
x: T-cell receptors bind antigen fragments presented on the surface of body cells, such as macrophages or infected cells. B cells can bind free antigen directly.

q: Which pairing of an immune cell with its role is correct?
o: Plasma cell — kills infected cells directly
Helper T cell — activates B cells and cytotoxic T cells
x: Helper T cells coordinate the response by activating other lymphocytes. Plasma cells secrete antibodies, cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells, and histamine comes from mast cells.

q: Why is the T-cell arm of specific defence described as 'cell-mediated'?
o: Antibodies dissolved in plasma do the work
Red blood cells carry the antigens away
T cells act directly on other cells themselves
The skin and mucous membranes block entry
x: In cell-mediated immunity T cells act themselves, for example by killing infected cells, rather than through antibodies released into body fluids.

q: A vaccine protects a person by:
o: Supplying ready-made antibodies from a horse
Killing all bacteria in the body at once
Stimulating the body to make its own antibodies and memory cells
x: A vaccine contains antigens that trigger the person's own immune response, leaving memory cells that give long-lasting protection. Ready-made antibodies give only passive immunity.

q: The BCG vaccine is given to protect against:
x: BCG (Bacillus Calmette–Guérin) is the vaccine against tuberculosis, usually given at birth.

q: AIDS is an example of:
x: AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) is caused by HIV, which weakens the immune system during life. It is not inherited, and the body is not attacking itself.

q: The first human disease to be wiped out worldwide by vaccination was:
x: Smallpox was declared eradicated by the WHO in 1980 after a worldwide vaccination campaign. Polio, measles and tuberculosis still occur.

q: A person has recovered from an infection with antigen X. Months later she meets antigen Y for the first time. Her response to Y will be:
o: A secondary response, because she already has memory cells
A primary response, because memory cells for X do not recognise Y
No response, because her lymphocytes are used up
Immediate, because antibodies against X also bind Y
x: Memory cells and antibodies are specific to the antigen that made them. Antigen Y needs its own clones to be selected, so the response is a slow primary one.

q: A baby is breast-fed and was also given the BCG vaccine at birth. The baby therefore has:
o: Natural active immunity and artificial passive immunity
Natural passive immunity and artificial active immunity
x: Antibodies received in breast milk give natural passive immunity. The vaccine makes the baby's own immune system respond, which is artificial active immunity.

q: After a kidney transplant, a patient takes drugs that suppress the immune system. An expected side effect is:
o: Faster rejection of the new kidney
x: The drugs reduce rejection by weakening the T-cell response, but this also weakens defence against pathogens, so infections become more likely.

q: A newborn mouse has its thymus removed. As it grows, which effect is expected?
o: It cannot make any red blood cells
Few mature T cells form, so cell-mediated immunity is very weak
It has more helper T cells than normal
Its B cells cannot form in the bone marrow
x: T cells mature in the thymus, so without it few functional T cells develop. B cells still arise in the bone marrow, though without helper T cells their antibody response is also poorer.

q: IgM is a pentamer made of five basic antibody units. How many antigen-binding sites does one IgM molecule have?
x: Each basic Y-shaped unit has two binding sites. Five units joined together give 5 × 2 = 10 antigen-binding sites.

q: Antibodies in the plasma cannot reach a virus once it is inside a body cell. The infection is then controlled mainly by:
o: Plasma cells entering the infected cells
Cytotoxic T cells destroying the infected cells
Red blood cells absorbing the virus
Memory B cells digesting the virus
x: Viruses inside cells are hidden from antibodies. Cytotoxic T cells recognise viral antigens displayed on the infected cell's surface and kill the cell, stopping the virus from multiplying.

q: Arrange the steps by which T cells clear a virus infection in their proper sequence:
o: Cytotoxic T cells multiply → antigen displayed by a macrophage → helper T cell activated → infected cells killed
Helper T cell activated → infected cells killed → antigen displayed by a macrophage → cytotoxic T cells multiply
Antigen displayed by a macrophage → helper T cell activated → cytotoxic T cells multiply → infected cells killed
Infected cells killed → cytotoxic T cells multiply → helper T cell activated → antigen displayed by a macrophage
x: A macrophage first presents the antigen, which activates helper T cells. Their cytokines make matching cytotoxic T cells divide into a clone, and these kill the infected cells.
